paras: The shooting at Will Nevels was an incident on the night of Thursday, 23 August 1900, in which Jim Bryan, a deputy of Constable Ed. Potter, fired a pistol at Nevels, a Black man, near the gas house in the Fourth ward of Raleigh, North Carolina. The shot missed, and the mayor issued a warrant for the deputy's arrest, which led the Raleigh News & Observer to report the case under the headline "Arrested a Deputy."

According to the News & Observer, Bryan was standing on a corner with his pistol in his hand when he saw Nevels and ordered him to come over. Nevels refused, saying, "I aint coming when you got that pistol in your hand." The paper supposed that Bryan "probably made a motion towards him," because Nevels then broke and ran. Bryan fired at once, and the ball split a panel in the fence beside which Nevels was running; no injury was reported.
The report gives no reason for Bryan's order and does not say that Nevels was suspected of any offense.

Mayor Powell "promptly issued a warrant for Bryan's arrest," and by the time the item went to press the warrant was "in the hands of the police force." Although the headline said the deputy had been arrested, the text does not state that the warrant had been served, and no report of a hearing or trial was found.

The only known account is a short item in the local news on page 5 of the Raleigh News & Observer of 25 August 1900. The paper led with the warrant rather than the shooting and quoted Nevels's own explanation for refusing the deputy's command. In the conventions of the time, it gave the deputy the honorific "Mr. Jim Bryan" while identifying Nevels only as "a negro."
No other white paper and no Black paper is known to have carried the story.
